content: Rewarming the Baby: To rewarm a baby, use skin-to-skin contact by placing the baby on the mother’s chest. General Baby Care: Always wash your hands thoroughly before and after handling the baby. Do not share baby care supplies, such as towels or feeding equipment, between babies to prevent cross-contamination. Umbilical Cord Care: Wash your hands before and after caring for the umbilical cord. Do not apply any substances or medications to the cord stump. Fold the diaper below the cord stump to keep it dry and exposed to air. Cover the cord stump loosely with clean clothing. If the cord stump becomes soiled, clean it with clean water and soap, then dry it thoroughly with a clean cloth. If the umbilical area becomes red, drains pus, or bleeds, examine the baby and manage the condition appropriately. Advise the mother to seek medical care immediately if these signs occur. Do not bandage the cord stump or the baby’s abdomen. Avoid unnecessary touching of the cord stump. Sleeping Guidelines: Use a bed net to protect the baby from insects during sleep, both day and night. Place the baby to sleep on their back or side. Keep the baby away from smoke or individuals who are smoking. Hygiene and Bathing: At birth, only remove blood or meconium from the baby’s skin. Do not remove the vernix (a protective layer on the baby’s skin). Do not bathe the baby until they are at least six hours old. Later, at home, wash the baby’s face, neck, and underarms daily. Clean the buttocks when soiled and dry thoroughly. Bathe the baby only when necessary, ensuring the room is warm and free of drafts. Use warm water for bathing, and thoroughly dry, dress, and cover the baby afterward. Do not bathe the baby if they are cold or less than six hours old. Do not apply anything to the baby’s eyes except an antimicrobial ointment at birth. Breastfeeding and Feeding Care: Breastfeeding should begin within one hour of birth. Babies should not receive any other food or drink before starting breastfeeding. Exclusive breastfeeding is recommended for the first six months of life. Breast milk contains all the nutrients a baby needs, is easily digestible, and provides protection against infections. Breastfeeding supports the baby’s development and strengthens the bond between mother and baby. It may also help delay a new pregnancy. Expressing Breast Milk: Teach the mother how to express breast milk using clean containers such as a wide-necked jug, jar, or bowl. Once expressed, the milk should be stored in a container with a well-fitting lid and labeled with the baby’s name, date, and time. To express milk, the mother should wash her hands thoroughly, sit or stand comfortably, and hold a clean container under her breast. She should place her thumb and first finger on either side of the areola, press slightly inward, and express milk by alternating sides for 20–30 minutes. If milk flow is poor, warm compresses, back and neck massage, or breast massage can help. Feed the baby immediately or store the milk in a cool, clean, and safe place. If the mother is not breastfeeding at all, she should express milk at least eight times in 24 hours to relieve pain and maintain milk supply. Cup Feeding: Teach the mother to feed the baby using a cup. She should measure the milk, hold the baby semi-upright, and rest the cup lightly on the baby’s lower lip. Milk should be tipped gently to the baby’s lips without pouring it into their mouth. The baby will suck and swallow the milk, and feeding should continue until the baby closes their mouth or shows no interest in taking more. If the baby does not take the calculated amount, feed for a longer time or more frequently. Monitor the baby’s intake over 24 hours. Signs of Adequate Milk Intake: The baby appears satisfied after feeding. Weight loss is less than 10% in the first week of life. The baby gains at least 160 grams per week or a minimum of 300 grams in the first month. The baby wets diapers as frequently as they are fed. Newborn Resuscitation: If the baby is not breathing or gasping for breath, begin resuscitation within one minute of birth. Clamp and cut the umbilical cord, then transfer the baby to a dry, clean, and warm surface. Inform the mother about the baby’s condition and the steps being taken to assist with breathing. Keep the baby wrapped and under a radiant heater if possible. Position the baby’s head slightly extended, and suction the mouth and nose if there is meconium-stained fluid or excessive secretions. If the baby still does not breathe, ventilate using a mask and bag, ensuring a proper seal and observing chest rise. Ventilate at 40 squeezes per minute for one minute, then reassess the heart rate. If the heart rate is less than 100 beats per minute or breathing is inadequate, continue ventilation and arrange for immediate referral to a hospital. Administering Medications: Administer 1 mg of vitamin K intramuscularly to all newborns one hour after birth to prevent bleeding disorders. If the baby is at risk of infection, administer intramuscular antibiotics (ampicillin and gentamicin) in the thigh for five days. Use a new syringe and needle for each antibiotic dose. Immunization and Preventive Care: Provide routine immunizations as per the schedule. If the mother tested positive for syphilis (RPR positive), administer a single dose of intramuscular benzathine penicillin to the baby. For possible gonococcal eye infections, administer a single dose of intramuscular antibiotics. Follow-Up and Seeking Care: Advise the mother to attend routine and follow-up visits for the baby’s health. Instruct the mother to seek immediate medical care if the baby shows signs of illness, such as difficulty breathing, fever, or poor feeding. Breastfeeding Counseling: Explain the importance of exclusive breastfeeding during pregnancy and after birth. Include the partner or other family members in the discussion if possible. Help the mother initiate breastfeeding within one hour of birth by placing the baby on her chest in skin-to-skin contact. Teach the mother correct positioning and attachment for breastfeeding to ensure effective feeding and prevent complications.
